raw:
The blue volume comes upstairs with you. By the time the house has settled into its nighttime creaks, it rests beside the lamp and the framed letter on your desk.

Lightning whitens the gardens once or twice beyond the window. Then you sleep.

Morning brings a low wash of cloud below the plateau and a basin of cold water in your room. Washed and dressed, you make your way downstairs with enough time to spare before orientation.

Breakfast is less ceremonial than dinner: dark coffee, eggs, oat porridge, smoked fish, bread still warm from the kitchen. A printed schedule lies beside the jam.

Thessaly studies it over a piece of toast. “This calls the first hour a welcoming address. Why not say who is addressing us?”

“Because the Chancellor may add someone,” Aldric says.

Caelindra, reading the same sheet without looking up, says, “Or because the printer has a taste for vagueness.”

Ysolde stands near the window with a plate of smoked fish, looking out toward the western bridge where the clouds have begun to pull apart. Seraphel sits quietly near the end of the table, her notebook closed beside her cup.

When the bell marks the quarter hour, the house begins to empty again.

The Conclave seminar room is across the quadrangle, its oval table set beneath framed copies of the Accords in seven scripts. Ashara and Rashid are already seated when you enter; both have papers laid before them. The remaining students filter in behind you.

At one end of the table, Chancellor Mordecai Ashworth closes a black folder and waits until the last chair is occupied.

“Good morning,” he says. “Today is for names, rooms, timetables, and the tedious mechanisms by which an institution hopes to keep you alive long enough to disagree with it productively.”
